description:
Fashioncore (sometimes also written as Fashionxcore or FXC ) is a fashion style emerged in the early 2000s, with its origins traceable to the late 1990s Hardcore Punk and related music scenes. The term initially originated as a tongue-in-cheek or outright derogatory label used within the hardcore scene to describe bands that, alongside their music, emphasized a dark and stylized look. This look drew from influences such as Horror Punk and Glam Rock . [ 1 ]

As the label spread, it became attached to a recognizable youth subculture whose participants were sometimes called "Fashioncore kids." Outside of hardcore punk circles, however, mainstream media repeatedly mislabeled the style as " emo ," which in turn produced the terms "new emo kids" or "fake emos" as a way of distinguishing the fashion-conscious hardcore look from the emo subculture it was being lumped in with.

The distinction mattered to those inside the scene. Traditional emo carried associations of sincere sensitivity and introspection, while the "fake emo" or Fashioncore look pushed those same signifiers into exaggeration, incorporating gloomier iconography inspired by goth culture, including references to self-harm and suicide that were themselves controversial within the goth scene. [ 1 ]

By the mid-2000s, the style had spread well beyond its hardcore origins. As it did, a split developed: some who had adopted the look moved toward the emerging Scene subculture, whose musical and visual priorities were diverging heavily from the early hardcore roots. Bands like Tokio Hotel and Avril Lavigne began appearing as reference points, which for many original participants marked the point where the two crowds had fully separated.
culturalContext: Key values (per the Aesthetics Wiki): Deliberate fashion presentation within a scene that traditionally rejected it; looking good in the mosh pit
